strengths: Novel and mathematically principled formulation of personalized treatment design as a constrained conditional black-box optimization problem, with clean derivations (Lagrangian dual, closed-form design-collapse and probabilistic sampling results) that connect LLM sampling entropy and an adversarial source critic to a coherent optimization objective.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 5 distinct real-world-derived clinical tasks (Warfarin, HIV, Breast, Lung, ADR) spanning discrete and continuous design spaces, compared against 10 baselines including both classical (gradient ascent, CMA-ES, GA, BO-qEI, simulated annealing) and LLM-based (LLAMBO, OPRO, Eureka) optimizers, plus Majority and Human baselines.

Exceptionally thorough ablation studies (12 in the appendix) covering backbone LLM choice, batch size, temperature, Wasserstein bound, certainty parameters, distribution-shift severity, surrogate/oracle evaluation budgets, prior-knowledge quality (including a carefully constructed and expert-verified adversarial knowledge condition), embedding model choice, and equivalence relation definition — this level of rigor is uncommon and substantially strengthens the empirical claims.

Theoretical justification (Theorem D.1) motivating why bounding 1-Wasserstein distance to the source distribution provides a generalization bound on the surrogate's test risk, connecting the algorithmic design choice to a principled error-bound argument.

Careful attention to reproducibility (public datasets for two tasks, detailed prompts, full pseudocode) and to responsible research practice (explicit ethics statement, discussion of hallucination/misinformation risks, physician-in-the-loop caveat), along with cost/carbon/GPU analyses that are rarely included in similar papers.
weaknesses: Two of the five evaluation tasks and the 'ground-truth' oracle functions for Breast, Lung, and ADR are themselves machine learning models (not real observed clinical outcomes), and the ADR task in particular is constructed by converting a classification label into a continuous objective via an ad hoc jittering scheme; this makes the evaluation partly simulation-based, which weakens the strength of claims about real-world clinical validity despite the 'real-world optimization tasks' framing.

Two tasks depend on proprietary/internal datasets (Flatiron and an unnamed internal clinical trial for ADR), limiting full reproducibility and independent verification, and the paper cannot disclose key details (drug/ADR identity) which limits transparency of some ablation results.

The best performance is achieved with closed-source, API-only models (o4-Mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o-mini), which the paper itself flags as a data-privacy/practicality concern for real clinical deployment, and open-source alternatives lag noticeably behind — this somewhat undercuts the practical significance of the proposed method for the target application.

The heavy theoretical apparatus (equivalence classes, entropy constraints, Lagrangian duality) ultimately reduces to a fairly simple procedural recipe (cluster by embedding similarity, weight by soft-max scores, iteratively update two scalar multipliers), and the ablations show considerable sensitivity to implementation choices (embedding model, batch size, temperature, W0), suggesting the 'principled' derivation may be somewhat over-engineered relative to the practical robustness of the final heuristic.

Evaluation reports a single proposed design per patient scored against a learned oracle rather than any real clinical trial or expert-adjudicated outcome, and statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals or hypothesis tests comparing LEON to the next-best baseline) is largely absent from the main results table despite reporting SEMs.

The knowledge-synthesis pipeline (Algorithm 2) is shown to be vulnerable to factually incorrect information (as demonstrated by the qualitative examples and adversarial-knowledge ablation), which is a fundamental risk for a method intended to eventually support treatment recommendations, and mitigation beyond 'careful vetting' and 'physician oversight' is not concretely proposed.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous mathematical formulation of the constrained black-box optimization problem, including full derivations (Lagrangian duality, design collapse, probabilistic sampling over equivalence classes) in the appendix.

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive, spanning 5 tasks, 10 baselines, and over a dozen ablation studies (batch size, temperature, Wasserstein bound, certainty parameters, distribution shift severity, evaluation budgets, knowledge quality/adversarial knowledge, reflection, embedding models, equivalence relations).

The adversarial and 'no-knowledge' knowledge-source ablations, together with physician/medical-student annotation of LLM-generated prior knowledge, are a thoughtful attempt to probe factual reliability of the method.

The paper includes a theoretical justification (Theorem D.1) motivating why bounding the 1-Wasserstein distance controls test-time extrapolation error, connecting the method to a concrete generalization argument.
Cost, carbon, and GPU utilization analyses, along with a reasonably candid limitations and ethics discussion, reflect an effort toward practical transparency.
weaknesses: The central evaluation design is questionable: for most tasks (HIV, Breast, Lung, ADR) the 'ground-truth objective' f used for final evaluation is itself just another fitted ML model (ResNet/GBDT) trained on a different data split, not real patient outcomes—so the headline results largely reflect agreement between two learned models under an artificially engineered covariate/label shift rather than genuine clinical validity.

The ADR task relies on an internal proprietary dataset with redacted drug/disease identities and no public access, and the paper's reproducibility statement leaves code and data-access links blank/redacted, undermining reproducibility of a substantial fraction of the results.

Several headline comparisons in Table 1 show overlapping standard errors (e.g., Warfarin: LEON 1.36±0.13 vs. BO-qEI 1.36±0.13; Grad. 1.37±0.13) with no significance testing reported, making the claimed 'average rank of 1.2' somewhat overstated relative to the actual uncertainty in the estimates.

The method is highly complex, with many moving, hand-tuned components (equivalence-class clustering, per-task natural-language templates for embeddings, source critic training/Lipschitz clipping, λ/μ updates, reflection prompting), raising concerns about practical usability and the engineering effort needed to adapt LEON to a new clinical task.

The main results use gpt-4o-mini as backbone, yet the paper's own ablation shows reasoning models (o4-mini, Gemini-2.5 Flash) and specialized embedding models (Bio+Clinical BERT) meaningfully outperform the reported configuration, suggesting the main-text numbers understate/misrepresent the method's best achievable performance and complicating direct comparison to baselines that were not similarly tuned.

Practical deployment via proprietary third-party LLM APIs (as needed for best performance) directly conflicts with the patient-privacy concerns the paper itself raises, and the paper does not propose or test a viable path to reconcile this tension.

The Majority baseline outperforming LEON on the ADR task, combined with the qualitative acknowledgment of class imbalance, suggests the method's core entropy/certainty machinery does not robustly generalize across all task types.

Strong LLM-based and biomedical-optimization baselines (e.g., protein/sequence-design LLM optimizers, evolutionary LLM approaches) are excluded due to implementation-generalization difficulty, weakening the claim that LEON outperforms 'LLM-based methods' in general rather than just the three re-implemented baselines chosen.

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: the paper formalizes personalized treatment optimization as a constrained black-box optimization problem and derives a principled closed-form solution (Lemma 4.2, 4.3, Corollary 4.4) that dynamically estimates both a source-critic certainty parameter (λ) and an LLM entropy-based certainty parameter (μ) without requiring hand-tuned hyperparameters, which is a meaningful advance over prior work that fixes these values or imposes restrictive assumptions.

Extensive and realistic empirical evaluation across 5 distinct real-world clinical optimization tasks (Warfarin, HIV, Breast, Lung, ADR) that each simulate genuine distribution shift scenarios (covariate and label shift), compared against 10 baselines including both traditional (gradient ascent, CMA-ES, GA, BO-qEI) and LLM-based (LLAMBO, OPRO, Eureka) optimizers, with LEON achieving the best average rank.

Very thorough ablation studies (12 distinct ablations in the appendix) covering backbone LLM choice, batch size, temperature, Wasserstein bound, certainty parameter necessity, distribution shift severity, evaluation budgets, prior knowledge quality (including a carefully constructed adversarial knowledge condition verified by clinical experts), reflection, and equivalence relation/embedding choices — this level of rigor substantially strengthens the credibility of the claimed contributions.

Thoughtful and expert-verified qualitative analysis of LLM-generated prior knowledge (annotated by a resident physician and senior medical student), providing transparency about both correct and incorrect generated content, which is a valuable contribution to understanding LLM reliability in this domain.
Theoretical justification (Theorem D.1) connecting the 1-Wasserstein distance bound to a formal generalization error bound, grounding the design choice in learning theory rather than pure heuristics.
Clear discussion of limitations, ethical considerations, cost/carbon footprint, and reproducibility, reflecting mature and responsible research practices.
weaknesses: Some of the datasets (Flatiron oncology data and the proprietary ADR dataset) are not fully publicly available, which somewhat limits full reproducibility of results on 3 of the 5 benchmark tasks despite the code being released.

The 'equivalence class' formalism relies on strong simplifying assumptions (finiteness of equivalence classes, coercivity/continuity of the combined surrogate-critic function) that may not strictly hold in high-dimensional or continuous clinical design spaces, and the practical equivalence relation (embedding + clustering) is somewhat heuristic relative to the clean theoretical formulation.
On the ADR task, LEON underperforms the trivial Majority baseline, and the paper's explanation (class imbalance) is somewhat post-hoc rather than analyzed rigorously within the framework.

The main results rely on a single LLM backbone (GPT-4o-mini) with no confidence intervals or significance testing reported for the primary comparison table beyond SEM, and while backbone ablations are provided in the appendix, performance differences across LLMs (e.g., Llama models performing markedly worse) suggest the method's advantage may be sensitive to the base model's inherent capability rather than purely the LEON framework.

The method introduces considerable algorithmic and implementation complexity (source critic training, dual parameter updates, equivalence class estimation, knowledge retrieval pipeline, reflection), which may hinder practical adoption and increases the surface area for subtle implementation errors relative to simpler baselines.

strengths: Provides a mathematically principled formulation of personalized treatment design as a constrained black-box optimization problem, with a full derivation (Lagrangian dual, design collapse lemma, closed-form probabilistic sampling rule) connecting LLM sampling entropy and an adversarial source critic to theoretically motivated 'certainty' parameters (λ, µ), and a supporting generalization bound (Theorem D.1) motivating the Wasserstein constraint.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 5 distinct, realistic clinical optimization tasks (Warfarin dosing, HIV ART regimen selection, breast/lung cancer treatment planning, ADR risk) with meaningful covariate/label distribution shift baked into the experimental design, compared against 10 baselines including LLM-based and traditional optimizers plus Majority/Human anchors.

Very thorough ablation and robustness analysis (backbone LLM choice, batch size, temperature, Wasserstein bound, λ/µ fixing, distribution shift severity, evaluation budgets, knowledge source quality/adversarial knowledge, reflection, equivalence relation/embedding/class-count choices, iterative vs. non-iterative), which substantially strengthens confidence in the reported gains and clarifies which components actually matter.

Additional analyses beyond raw performance—cost/carbon footprint, qualitative and quantitative auditing of LLM-generated prior knowledge by clinical experts, and a preliminary subgroup fairness analysis by gender/race—demonstrate unusually comprehensive scientific rigor for an applied ML paper.

Clear discussion of limitations, ethics, and a candid negative result (LEON underperforms Majority on ADR due to class imbalance), and thoughtful theoretical discussion of extending the framework to multi-objective settings.
weaknesses: The 'ground-truth objective' functions for most tasks (HIV, Breast, Lung, ADR) are themselves learned ML models (ResNet/GBDT) trained on a separate 'target' dataset rather than true clinical outcomes; framing these as an oracle somewhat overstates what is actually being validated (agreement between two proxy models rather than real-world efficacy).

The task_description prompts explicitly tell the LLM which patient subgroup the surrogate is known to be inaccurate for (e.g., 'trained on White patients only'); this hands all LLM-based methods precise foreknowledge of the exact axis of distribution shift, which is unlikely to be available in real deployments and may partly explain the strong relative gains of LLM-based approaches over non-LLM baselines.

Reproducibility is limited for 2 of 5 tasks (Breast/Lung data from Flatiron Health, ADR proprietary internal trial data) with contact-based rather than open access, and specific redacted identifiers (drug names, disease) reduce external verifiability of the ADR results.

The method has many interacting hyperparameters and design choices (W0, ηλ, ηcritic, equivalence relation type/embedding model/class count, batch size, temperature, reflection), and while ablations are extensive, the sheer number of tunable components raises concerns about implicit overfitting to the specific benchmark suite despite claims of no task-specific tuning.

Qualitative knowledge audits reveal that LLM-synthesized 'prior knowledge' can be factually incorrect (e.g., reversed VKORC1 dosing guidance) even from reputable-seeming knowledge tools, and the ADR-task adversarial-knowledge ablation shows the method can be meaningfully degraded by misinformation—an important safety caveat for a method proposed for personalized medicine, even though the authors are appropriately transparent about this limitation.

Evaluation is based on n=100 patients per task with mostly point estimates ± SEM; aside from the fairness analysis, limited formal significance testing (e.g., paired tests against baselines) is reported for the main Table 1 comparisons, making some close margins (e.g., vs. BO-qEI/Grad. on Warfarin) hard to interpret statistically.

The multi-objective extension, which would be practically important for realistic clinical decision-making (balancing efficacy vs. toxicity vs. cost), is discussed only theoretically in the appendix without any empirical validation.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important problem: leveraging LLM prior/domain knowledge to mitigate surrogate model unreliability under distribution shift in personalized medicine, a well-motivated setting given documented underrepresentation of certain populations in clinical data.

The theoretical derivation (Lagrangian relaxation, design collapse lemma, closed-form sampling distribution over equivalence classes, dual ascent update for the source-critic weight) is internally consistent and clearly presented with full proofs in the appendix.

Extremely extensive empirical appendix: ablations on backbone LLM, batch size, temperature, Wasserstein bound, certainty parameters, equivalence relation/embedding choice, number of equivalence classes, reflection, knowledge source quality (including an adversarial misinformation study), subgroup fairness, cost/carbon accounting, and extension to non-LLM optimizers.

The method is evaluated on 5 distinct real-world-motivated clinical tasks (Warfarin, HIV, Breast, Lung, ADR) spanning continuous and discrete design spaces, with a reasonably broad set of 10 baselines (traditional optimizers, Bayesian optimization, and LLM-based optimizers).
Honest limitations and ethics sections, including acknowledgment of sensitivity to knowledge quality and the fact that the method is not intended for direct clinical use.
weaknesses: Core theoretical contribution has questionable value: the 'Design Collapse' lemma and the derivation of q̄ as a softmax over equivalence-class maxima essentially reduce to greedy per-class scoring with a Gibbs-style reweighting; the heavy Lagrangian/dual machinery (Sections 4.2–4.4, Appendix A) produces a method that in practice just rescales candidate scores by two scalar multipliers (λ, μ) fit via simple heuristics (linear regression, one-step gradient descent) — the mathematical formalism appears to overstate the technical depth relative to what is algorithmically implemented.

The entire framework hinges on a user-defined, somewhat arbitrary equivalence relation ∼ (operationalized via k-means clustering of text embeddings with an ad hoc 'elbow method' for choosing N). This is a critical, non-trivial design choice that is justified only empirically post-hoc (Appendix E.11-E.13) rather than motivated theoretically, undermining the 'mathematically principled' claim in the abstract.

Evaluation scale is small and effect sizes are often within noise: n=100 patients per task, with largely overlapping confidence intervals between LEON and several baselines (e.g., Warfarin: LEON 1.36±0.13 vs Grad./BO-qEI 1.36-1.37±0.13; HIV: differences in the third decimal with heavily overlapping SEMs). The claimed 'average rank of 1.2' is driven by consistent small wins across tasks rather than large, statistically convincing margins, and no formal significance testing (e.g., paired tests across patients) is reported for the main results in Table 1.

Several tasks rely on proprietary/inaccessible data (ADR task, Breast/Lung via Flatiron Health) and the paper's reproducibility statement defers to institutional contacts rather than providing a usable released dataset, limiting independent verification of the central claims.

The construction of the ADR task objective is artificial: a predictive classification task is converted into an optimization problem via an invented perturbation/jitter scheme (Appendix C.1) with an injected index-matching constraint; it's unclear this transformation preserves meaningful clinical semantics, and this is the task where LEON is actually beaten by the trivial Majority baseline in the main results.

The 'knowledgeable' aspect of the method is essentially a RAG/tool-calling wrapper (Supplementary Algorithm 2) bolted onto a standard prompting-based optimizer (OPRO-style), and the ablation in Appendix D.11 shows that simply adding the same knowledge-generation step to baseline methods (OPRO, Eureka) closes much of the performance gap — undermining the narrative that the constrained optimization formulation (the paper's main theoretical contribution) is what drives the improvement, since knowledge alone pushes OPRO/Eureka much closer to LEON in rank.

LEON offers no meaningful benefit when combined with non-LLM optimizers (Appendix D.7), and the paper's own interpretation is that prior knowledge is 'critical,' which raises the question of whether the elaborate constrained-optimization/entropy formalism is doing real work beyond providing a scaffold for knowledge injection.

The backbone LLM ablation (Table S5) shows substantial performance variance across models, with the primary paper result (GPT-4o-mini) not being the best-performing configuration, suggesting the main table results are somewhat cherry-picked/model-dependent rather than representing a robust method.

Baseline comparisons may not be fully fair: LLAMBO, OPRO, and Eureka are evaluated without access to the knowledge-generation module in the main Table 1 (by the authors' own admission), making the headline comparison partially confounded by unequal information access rather than purely algorithmic superiority.

Clinical validity of the underlying evaluation framework is questionable: ground-truth 'oracle' functions for Breast/Lung/ADR are themselves machine learning models trained on limited data (GBDT with R² values that can be negative off-distribution per Fig. S1), meaning the entire evaluation rests on potentially unreliable proxy objectives for both the surrogate and the 'ground truth,' which the distribution-shift analysis itself seems to confirm (e.g., negative R² for source model on Breast/Lung).

The qualitative prior-knowledge analysis (Appendix D.4) itself documents instances of factually incorrect LLM-generated medical knowledge propagating into the optimization pipeline, raising safety concerns inadequately addressed beyond a boilerplate limitations paragraph, especially given the paper positions this for 'personalized medicine.'

strengths: Strong theoretical grounding: the paper derives a principled constrained optimization formulation (entropy + Wasserstein/source-critic constraints) with full proofs (Lemmas 4.2/4.3, Corollary 4.4), connecting LLM sampling entropy to a Lagrangian dual framework in a mathematically rigorous way that is uncommon in the 'LLM-as-optimizer' literature.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 5 realistic, diverse personalized medicine tasks (Warfarin, HIV, Breast, Lung, ADR) with distribution shift explicitly constructed between source/target populations, which is a practically important and underexplored setting.

Extensive baselines (10 methods spanning classical optimizers, Bayesian optimization, and LLM-based optimizers) and an unusually thorough appendix with ablations (temperature, batch size, Wasserstein bound, certainty parameters, embedding models, equivalence relations, number of equivalence classes, reflection, backbone LLM, knowledge sources including adversarial knowledge).

Thoughtful qualitative analysis including expert (physician/medical student) annotation of LLM-generated prior knowledge for factual correctness, a fairness subgroup analysis, cost/carbon accounting, and a theoretical generalization bound (Theorem D.1) motivating the Wasserstein constraint.

The method is practically appealing: no fine-tuning required, works in a prompting-only setup, and the ablations show the gains are attributable to the proposed constrained formulation (dynamic λ/µ) rather than knowledge alone (Table S4), strengthening the causal claim of the contribution.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol has questionable realism: surrogate and 'ground-truth' objective functions are both learned/approximate models (e.g., GBDT or ResNet trained on different data splits) rather than true clinical outcomes, so the 'ground truth' evaluator itself may have substantial error, undermining strong claims like 'LEON proposes treatments superior to retrospective clinician choices.'

Evaluation budget (2048 surrogate evaluations) and reliance on single final design evaluation may not reflect realistic clinical constraints, and the online (no-shift) ablation (E.6) suggests LEON's advantage shrinks or disappears without distribution shift, raising concern that gains are narrowly tied to the synthetic shift construction rather than general optimizer superiority.

The entropy/equivalence-class framework depends heavily on an engineering choice (k-means clustering on text embeddings with heuristic cluster count via elbow method) that is somewhat ad hoc relative to the elegant theory; the ablations (Table S9, S10) show meaningful sensitivity to embedding model and class count, suggesting the practical realization is less principled than the surrounding math implies.

Correctness verification of LLM-generated prior knowledge was done manually by only two annotators on a small number of qualitative examples (Warfarin only), which is insufficient to support general claims about knowledge reliability across all 5 tasks and could reflect confirmation/selection bias in which examples were highlighted.

Many ablations (e.g., λ/µ ablation, knowledge quality ablation) use only n=100 patients with fairly large standard errors and overlapping confidence intervals between conditions (e.g., Table S6, S10), making some comparative claims (e.g., 'Elbow consistently better') statistically fragile.

The proprietary ADR dataset and redacted drug/disease identities reduce reproducibility and external verifiability of one of the five core benchmark tasks; similarly Breast/Lung data (Flatiron) require data use agreements, limiting independent reproduction of the full benchmark suite despite the detailed reproducibility statement.
